issues.legal_issue: Premises let for residence but used by the tenant for professional purposes with the landlord’s consent are not recoverable on the ground that the landlord bona fide requires them for residence.
material_facts: A substantial part of the premises had been used by the tenant for his medical profession from the beginning of the tenancy.
The tenant’s professional use was with the landlord’s consent.
The landlord sought possession for his own residential use, but the courts below found that the premises were not let for residence alone.
issues.conclusion: The landlord was not entitled to eject the tenant under Section 13(1)(e), even if the landlord established a bona fide residential need.
issues.legal_principle: Under the explanation to Section 13(1)(e) of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, premises let for residence but used incidentally for professional or other purposes with the landlord’s consent fall outside the category of premises let for residential purposes alone. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.residential_need_ejectment_claim: The landlord seeks possession of the premises on the ground of a need to occupy them as a residence.
predicates.residential_let: The premises were let for use as a residence.
predicates.professional_use_with_landlord_consent: The tenant used the premises for professional purposes with the landlord’s consent.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks possession for residential need and premises let for residence are used professionally with the landlord’s consent, the landlord cannot eject the tenant on residential need alone.

issues.legal_issue: Premises let for both residential and commercial or professional purposes remain within the statutory definition of premises.
material_facts: The premises were used by the tenant both as a residence and for his medical profession.
The landlord himself sought ejectment under the Act.
The landlord argued that the combined use placed the premises outside the Act’s definition of premises.
issues.conclusion: The combined residential and commercial or professional use did not take the premises outside Section 2(g); they remained premises within the Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(g) includes premises let for residence, commercial use, or any other purpose. The Court held that the latter category includes premises let for combined residential and commercial or professional use. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.premises_definition_issue: A dispute concerns whether premises fall within a statutory definition covering premises let for residence, commercial use, or another purpose.
predicates.premises_let_for_combined_use: The premises were let for both residential and commercial or professional use.

issues.definition: When premises are let for combined residential and commercial or professional use, they remain within the statutory definition of premises.

issues.legal_issue: A tenancy used for both residence and professional purposes cannot be terminated merely because the tenant has acquired a suitable residence elsewhere.
material_facts: The tenant used the premises both for residence and for his medical profession.
The landlord sought ejectment on the ground that the tenant had acquired another suitable residence.
The tenant’s other residence would not meet the professional purpose for which the tenancy was also used.
issues.conclusion: The tenant could not be ejected under Section 13(1)(h) merely because he had acquired a suitable residence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(h) permits ejectment where the tenant has acquired a suitable residence. Where the tenancy is created or used for both residence and professional purposes, acquisition of premises suitable for residence alone does not satisfy the purposes of the tenancy and cannot alone justify its termination. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.acquisition_based_ejectment_claim: The landlord seeks possession on the ground that the tenant has acquired another suitable residence.
predicates.mixed_residential_professional_tenancy: The tenant’s premises are used for both residence and professional purposes.
predicates.tenant_acquired_suitable_residence: The tenant acquired premises suitable for residential use.

issues.definition: If a landlord seeks possession because the tenant acquired a suitable residence, but the tenancy serves both residential and professional purposes, the landlord cannot terminate it on that acquisition alone.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court will not entertain a new plea requiring further evidence when it is raised for the first time on appeal and the opposing party had no opportunity to meet it.
material_facts: The landlord argued for the first time before the Supreme Court that the tenant should not be allowed to claim that the tenancy covered professional as well as residential use because he had previously obtained extensions by describing it as residential.
The plea required relevant evidence, and the tenant had no opportunity to meet it because it had not been raised at the proper stage.
The parties’ earlier conduct included positions inconsistent with the positions they later advanced.
issues.conclusion: The landlord could not raise the new plea in the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the settled practice that new pleas requiring further evidence are not allowed in appeals under Article 136 of the Constitution, particularly where the opposing party had no opportunity to respond. No earlier cases were cited.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal and new_plea_raised_first_time and plea_requires_further_evidence and opposing_party_lacked_opportunity

predicates.special_leave_appeal: The matter is an appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.new_plea_raised_first_time: A party advances the plea for the first time in the appellate court.
predicates.plea_requires_further_evidence: Determining the plea requires evidence beyond the record already made.
predicates.opposing_party_lacked_opportunity: The opposing party had no opportunity at the proper stage to meet the plea.

issues.definition: In a special-leave appeal, a plea raised for the first time that requires further evidence will not be allowed when the opposing party had no opportunity to meet it.
